Rust has macros because it has no variadic generics and no reflection, and because a lot of Rust's ergonomics are syntactic. You will use macros far more often than you write them, but knowing how they work stops them feeling like magic.

Two families

Kind Example How
Declarative (macro_rules!) vec!, println!, matches! pattern-match on tokens
Procedural #[derive(Serialize)], sqlx::query! a function over a token stream

Procedural macros come in three flavours: derive macros, attribute macros, and function-like macros. They must live in their own crate with proc-macro = true.

macro_rules! basics

A macro rule is (matcher) => { expansion }. Fragments are typed by a fragment specifier:

Specifier Matches
expr any expression
ident an identifier
ty a type
pat a pattern
stmt a statement
block a { ... } block
item a function/struct/impl
literal a literal
tt a single token tree
meta an attribute's contents
path a a::b::C path

Multiple arms and repetition

  • $( ... )+ repeats one or more times, * zero or more, ? optional.
  • $(,)? accepts an optional trailing comma — always include it in list macros.
  • $($x:expr),+ means "one or more expr, separated by commas".

A more useful example: a hash map literal

Hygiene

Macro-introduced identifiers do not collide with caller identifiers:

$crate refers to the defining crate, which is essential in exported macros:

Without $crate, a caller with a different logger in scope breaks.

Derive macros

The compiler invokes a proc macro with the item's tokens and splices the result back. Writing one requires syn and quote:

syn parses Rust, quote builds Rust. Almost every derive macro in the ecosystem is this shape plus attribute parsing.

Attribute macros

An attribute macro receives the annotated item and returns a replacement. This is how #[tokio::main] turns an async fn main into a runtime plus block_on.

Function-like proc macros

query_as! connects to the database at compile time, checks the SQL, and infers the result type. A typo in a column name is a compile error. This is Rust's answer to "ORM or raw SQL?" — raw SQL with compile-time verification.

Other examples: serde_json::json!, include_str!, env!, format_args!.

Macros from the standard library you should know

dbg! is worth internalising: it prints [src/main.rs:12] value = 42 to stderr and returns the value, so you can drop it inline:

When to write a macro (rarely)

Write one when:

  • You need a variadic API (vec!, println!).
  • You must generate code from a list (impl_from! for 20 types).
  • You need compile-time verification against external data (sqlx::query!).
  • The alternative is a boilerplate impl repeated per type.

Do not write one when a generic function or trait would do. A macro has no type checking until it is expanded, no IDE support for its body, and errors point at the expansion site.

Debugging a macro

cargo expand is the single most useful tool when a derive macro misbehaves. Read the generated code, find the line that fails, fix the input.

A worked example: a time_it! macro

The __ prefix on introduced identifiers is convention — hygiene already protects them, but it signals intent to readers.

A worked example: generating From impls

One line per conversion instead of five. thiserror's #[from] does the same thing with less rope.

Exercises

  1. Write macro_rules! hashmap supporting k => v pairs, empty, and trailing comma. Test all three.
  2. Write macro_rules! unless — unless!(cond, { ... }) runs the block when cond is false.
  3. Write a min! macro that works with any number of arguments (at least one) using recursion or a fold over $( )*.
  4. Use cargo expand on a #[derive(Serialize)] struct and read the generated code.
  5. Convert a repeated impl From<X> for MyError block (five types) into a declarative macro and confirm ? still works.
  6. Explain why $crate matters in an exported macro.
